name: Dutch
family: Indo-European, Germanic, West Germanic, Low Franconian
variety: Northern Standard Dutch (the Netherlands); the main differences of Southern (Belgian) Standard Dutch are noted where they matter
sources: Gussenhoven, Carlos (1992). Dutch. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 22(1-2), 45-47. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.
Verhoeven, Jo (2005). Belgian Standard Dutch. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 35(2), 243-247.
Booij, Geert (1995). The Phonology of Dutch. Oxford University Press.
Collins, Beverley and Mees, Inger M. (2003). The Phonetics of English and Dutch. 5th edition. Leiden: Brill.
Pols, L. C. W.; Tromp, H. R. C.; Plomp, R. (1973). Frequency analysis of Dutch vowels from 50 male speakers. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 53(4), 1093-1101.
Adank, Patti; van Hout, Roeland; Smits, Roel (2004). An acoustic description of the vowels of Northern and Southern Standard Dutch. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 116(3), 1729-1738.
Lisker, Leigh and Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20(3), 384-422.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the Rhythm Class Hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

vowel_formants.speaker: mean of 50 adult male speakers from the Netherlands, vowels in h-vowel-t words
vowel_formants.source: Pols, Tromp and Plomp 1973 (means recomputed from the per-speaker data distributed with Praat)

contrasts: tense (long) versus lax (short) vowels, differing in quality and length: /aː/ versus /ɑ/ (maan versus man), /eː/ versus /ɪ/ and /ɛ/, /oː/ versus /ɔ/, /øː/ versus /ʏ/
front rounded vowels /y ʏ øː œy/ versus front unrounded and back rounded vowels
three true diphthongs /ɛi œy ɑu/ (ijs, huis, koud) versus the long mid vowels /eː øː oː/
voiced versus voiceless obstruents /b d v z ɣ/ versus /p t f s x/, neutralised at the end of a word
/ʋ/ versus /v/ versus /f/ (wee, vee, fee); for many northern speakers /v/ and /f/ merge word-initially
/x/ versus /ɣ/, kept in the south and largely merged in the north
schwa /ə/ as a separate unstressable vowel
lexical stress (vóórkomen 'to occur' versus voorkómen 'to prevent')
allophony: /eː øː oː/ are narrow closing diphthongs [ei øy ou] in the Netherlands and monophthongs in Belgium; before /r/ they are monophthongal or centring, about [ɪː øː ɔː] or [eə øə oə] (beer, deur, boor)
/i y u/ are phonetically short, except before /r/ in the same foot, where they are long [iː yː uː] (bier, vuur, boer)
/ɛi œy ɑu/ start lower in much present-day Netherlandic speech, about [ai ɒy ɑu] (Stroop 1998)

/r/ varies by region, speaker and position: alveolar tap or trill [ɾ r], uvular trill or fricative [ʀ ʁ], and in the coda, for many speakers in the west of the Netherlands, a retroflex or bunched approximant [ɻ]; coda /r/ may weaken to a vocalic offglide
/x ɣ/ are post-velar or uvular [x χ] in the north, usually both voiceless and with strong friction; in the south they are front-velar [x̟ ɣ̟] ('soft g') and keep the voicing contrast
/v z/ are weakly voiced; northern speakers often devoice them, above all word-initial /v/
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant [ʋ] in the north, bilabial [β̞] in the south, and [w]-like after a vowel (nieuw, leeuw)
/l/ is dark (velarised or pharyngealised) in the coda, and for many speakers in all positions
/p t k/ are unaspirated and /b d/ are prevoiced; /ɡ/ occurs in loans (goal) and as the voiced form of /k/ before a voiced stop (zakdoek [ˈzɑɡduk])
final devoicing: obstruents are voiceless at the end of a word (hond [ɦɔnt] beside honden [ˈɦɔndə(n)], heb [ɦɛp] beside hebben)
regressive voicing before /b d/ (opbellen [ˈɔbɛlə(n)], zakdoek) and progressive devoicing of a fricative after an obstruent (afval [ˈɑfɑl], opvallen [ˈɔpfɑlə(n)], het vee [ət feː])
/n/ after schwa is dropped in most speech (lopen [ˈloːpə])
schwa is inserted in coda clusters of /l r/ plus a non-coronal consonant (melk [ˈmɛlək], arm [ˈɑrəm], film [ˈfɪləm])
/sj zj tj nj/ are alveolo-palatal [ɕ ʑ c ɲ] (meisje, katje, oranje); [ʃ ʒ] occur in loans (chef, garage)
a glottal stop or creaky onset precedes a vowel-initial stressed syllable, also inside a word (beamen [bəˈʔaːmə(n)])
unstressed full vowels are often reduced to schwa in casual speech (banaan [bəˈnaːn], minuut [məˈnyt])
phonotactics: lax vowels /ɪ ʏ ɛ ɑ ɔ/ do not end a word or a stressed syllable; they need a following consonant
after a long vowel or diphthong the rhyme holds one further consonant, plus coronal obstruents (herfst [ɦɛrfst], koorts)
onset clusters of up to three consonants begin with /s/ (spr, str, spl, sxr: schrijven [ˈsxrɛivə(n)])
/ɦ/ only begins syllables; /ŋ/ only follows short vowels and never begins a word
no geminates: identical consonants that meet across a boundary are reduced to one (handdoek [ˈɦɑnduk])
syllables with schwa are never stressed
word-final obstruents are voiceless; voicing assimilation applies across word and compound boundaries

stress.type: lexical, weight-sensitive, within a three-syllable window
stress.rule: In simplex words stress falls on one of the last three syllables: on the penultimate by default, on a final superheavy syllable, never on a schwa syllable; native Germanic words stress the first syllable of the stem, and compounds stress their first member.
stress.cues: pitch movement when the word is accented, longer duration, and spectral balance (more energy in the higher frequencies); overall intensity is a weak cue; unstressed vowels may reduce to schwa

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: schwa is the usual vowel of unstressed native syllables, and unstressed full vowels are optionally reduced to schwa in casual speech
rhythm.notes: The nPVI value comes from one speaker reading a text.

length.notes: Length goes with quality: long /aː eː øː oː/ are about one and a half to two times as long as the lax vowels, while tense /i y u/ are short except before /r/. There are no long consonants.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Lisker and Abramson 1964 (one speaker, isolated words)

intonation.pitch_range: medium, narrower than in British English
intonation.declarative: hat pattern: a rise on the first accented syllable, a high stretch with gradual declination, and a fall on the last accented syllable to a low boundary (H* ... H*L L%)
intonation.yes_no_question: final rise to a high boundary (L*H H% or H* H%); questions with inversion may also fall
intonation.wh_question: accent on the question word and a falling nuclear accent with a low boundary; a final rise is optional
intonation.continuation: fall-rise or rise ending in a high boundary (H*L H% or L*H H%) at the end of a non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: H*L: peak in the accented syllable, with the fall completed in the next syllable; the accent-lending rise is early in the accented syllable and the accent-lending fall late in it
intonation.notes: Descriptions follow the IPO grammar of 't Hart, Collier and Cohen (1990) and the ToDI transcription of Gussenhoven (2005).

tone.notes: The standard language has no lexical tone (the Limburgish dialects do).

phonation: glottal stop or creaky voice at the onset of vowel-initial stressed syllables

problems: /r/ is always an alveolar trill (imported from base1/R2); neither the uvular variants nor the approximant used in the coda in the west of the Netherlands are available
/eː øː oː/ use closing-diphthong formant data also before /r/ (door, kleur), where the standard has monophthongal or centring vowels; only some words (meer, voor) get the special phonemes I: and O:
/i y u/ are not lengthened before /r/ (bier, vuur, boer use the short phonemes)
the marginal long vowels /ɛː œː ɔː/ are missing: crème comes out as [krɛmə], militair with short [ɛ], freule with [øː], zone with [oː]
progressive devoicing of fricatives is missing (afval [fv], opvallen [pv]) and regressive voicing is applied unevenly (zakdoek [ɡd] but opbellen [pb])
stress errors in compounds and particle verbs: huisdeur, ijsbeer, handdoek, zakdoek and opbellen are stressed on the second part; oranje is stressed on the first syllable
no schwa insertion in melk, film, arm, kalm
written g is a voiced velar [ɣ] and ch a strong [x] imported from Afrikaans: this matches neither the northern standard (both voiceless) nor the southern one (front-velar)
questions are given the same tune whether they are yes-no or wh-questions, because the tune is chosen from the question mark alone
good: final devoicing is applied (hond [hɔnt], heb [hɛp], goed [ɣut])
tense and lax vowels differ in both quality and length, and the three diphthongs [ɛi œy ɑu] have their own formant data
w is a labiodental approximant [ʋ] and /p t k/ are unaspirated
unstressed endings have schwa (mogelijk [ˈmoːɣələk], lelijk), and nj, sj coalesce (oranje [ɲ], sjaal [ʃ])
a short pause stands in for the glottal onset before word-initial and hiatus vowels (beamen, geërgerd)

notes: In the consonant list /ɡ ʃ ʒ/ are marginal (loans and assimilation products). In the vowel list /iː yː uː ɛː œː ɔː/ are marginal: the first three occur before /r/ and in loans (analyse, centrifuge), the last three only in loans (crème, freule, zone). The sequences aːi, oːi, ui, iu, yu, eːu in the diphthong list are vowel plus glide (haai, mooi, boei, nieuw, duw, leeuw). The formant values are from the 1960s and 1970s generation; Adank, van Hout and Smits (2004) give newer values for both national varieties.
